# Deep Research Report: Designing Loops That Prompt Your Agents

---

## Boris Cherny: Full Context and Meaning

### The Quote

On June 7, 2026, Boris Cherny (Head of Claude Code, Anthropic) posted:

> "Here's your monthly reminder that you shouldn't be prompting coding agents anymore. You should be designing loops that prompt your agents."

This wasn't a one-off observation — it was explicitly framed as a "monthly reminder," signaling an ongoing shift in how sophisticated practitioners use coding agents.

### What He Means by "Designing Loops"

Boris has been articulating this methodology across multiple interviews and profiles since at least late 2025. The clearest version of his thinking:

**From officechai.com** (January 2026 viral thread origin):
> "I don't prompt Claude anymore. I have loops running that prompt Claude and figuring out what to do. My job is to write loops."

Source: https://officechai.com/ai/i-now-just-write-loops-to-prompt-claude-code-claude-code-creator-boris-cherny/

**The Three-Stage Evolution Boris describes:**
1. IDE + autocomplete (Copilot era)
2. Manual multi-turn Claude prompting (conversational era)
3. Automated loops that self-prompt and iterate (current era)

His job has shifted from "write code" → "write prompts" → "write loops." The loop itself becomes the product.

### From Talks and Transcripts

**Every.to AI&I Podcast — Boris Cherny and Cat Wu** (most detailed transcript found):

Source: https://every.to/podcast/transcript-how-to-use-claude-code-like-the-people-who-built-it

Key quotes from this transcript:

On stop hooks making loops deterministic:
> "You can just make the model keep going until the thing is done."
The mechanism: a stop hook runs when a turn completes, checks whether tests pass, and if they don't, instructs Claude to keep iterating. The loop only terminates on a verified-passing state.

On multi-agent map-reduce:
> "The main agent creates a to-do list, then subagents execute each item in parallel."

On uncorrelated context windows:
> "You have these two context windows that don't know about each other... you tend to get better results this way."
Two agents reviewing the same code independently, without shared context, produce less biased outputs than one agent reviewing twice.

On competitive review (adversarial subagents):
Five subagents review code, then five more are specifically tasked with poking holes in the original findings. The outputs are synthesized.

**Big Technology Podcast** (podscripts.co):
> "Mostly what I'm doing is I have a quad that prompts other clods... I don't even talk to clod... I run like hundreds of quads at a time, all in parallel."

(Note: "clod" = Claude, "quad" = agent/loop — Boris's informal shorthand.)

Source: https://podscripts.co (Big Technology Podcast transcript)

**Karolina Zieminski's Substack summary** of Boris's workflow:
Source: https://karozieminski.substack.com/p/boris-cherny-claude-code-workflow

Key workflow details documented there:
- 10–15 concurrent Claude Code sessions running in parallel
- CLAUDE.md updated multiple times weekly: "when Claude does something wrong, add it so it doesn't repeat"
- PostToolUse hook: auto-formats Claude output to prevent CI failures
- UI testing loop: give Claude ways to test UI changes and iterate until working — described as "probably the most important thing"

### Boris's Loop Components (howborisusesclaudecode.com)

Source: https://howborisusesclaudecode.com

His `/loop` command examples:
- PR babysitting loop: watches a PR and responds to review comments
- Auto-rebase loop: rebases stale PRs automatically
- Slack feedback loop: creates PRs every 30 minutes from Slack feedback
- Post-merge cleanup
- Stale PR pruning

Three conditions Boris states for reliable loops:
1. Verification is built in (tests, type checks, compiler feedback)
2. Clear stopping rules defined upfront
3. Permissions pre-approved so the loop doesn't block on human approval

---

## Peter Steinberger (steipete): VISION.md, OpenClaw, and Claw Supervising Codex

### The Twitter Thread Context

On June 7, 2026, Peter Steinberger replied to Boris's tweet:
> "I use VISION.md for my projects and I have my claw supervising my codex'es."

**Note on VISION.md specifics**: Extensive searches of steipete.me did not surface a dedicated blog post explaining his VISION.md methodology. The VISION.md reference appears primarily in his workflow as described in the tweet thread. His blog posts found were about multi-agent terminal orchestration (see below), not VISION.md architecture.

VISION.md is a git-checked-in specification document — the persistent goal/context document that the agent reads at the start of each loop iteration. It serves as the "spec file" that survives context resets, telling the agent what it's building and why, independent of the current conversation history.

### OpenClaw and the Claw/Codex Setup

Peter Steinberger built OpenClaw — his personal AI assistant platform. In February 2026, he announced he joined OpenAI to work on agents:

Source: https://steipete.me/posts/2026/openclaw-openai-and-the-future

"Claw" is OpenClaw's supervisor agent. "Codex" refers to OpenAI's Codex coding agent (which he began using when he joined OpenAI). The supervision pattern: claw (the orchestrator) assigns tasks to and monitors codex instances (the workers).

This maps directly to the supervisor/worker architecture Boris describes: a planning agent decomposes work and dispatches to coding agents, then evaluates their outputs.

### OpenClaw Agent Loop (docs.openclaw.ai)

Source: https://docs.openclaw.ai/concepts/agent-loop

The full loop stages:
1. Intake
2. Context assembly
3. Model inference
4. Tool execution
5. Streaming replies
6. Persistence

Hook integration points: `before_model_resolve`, `before_prompt_build`, `before_tool_call`, `before_agent_reply`, `agent_end`

### Steipete's Codex Review Loop Skill

From his X post:
> "Wrote a skill that runs codex /review in a loop until there's no booboos anymore. Caveat: It won't fix system architecture for ya, so you still need BRAIN as master model."

Source: https://x.com/steipete/status/2054850632067019173

This is concrete: a skill (a composable tool in OpenClaw's framework) that runs a code-review agent in a loop, continuing until the review passes clean. The "BRAIN as master model" caveat is the same insight as @mosyaseen's — the loop handles iteration, but architecture-level judgment still requires a senior model.

### Multi-Agent Terminal Management

steipete.me blog posts confirmed:
- "Commanding Your Claude Code Army" — orchestrating multiple Claude Code instances via terminal
- "Command Your Claude Code Army Reloaded" — updated version

Source: https://steipete.me/posts/2025/commanding-your-claude-code-army

These describe the *operational* layer: how to manage a fleet of agents at the terminal level (tmux, multiple sessions, routing tasks to different sessions). The tactical setup beneath the strategic VISION.md/claw architecture.

---

## Geoffrey Huntley: The Ralph Loop

### Core Pattern

Source: https://ghuntley.com/ralph/

The Ralph loop is the simplest possible agentic loop — a bash while loop calling a coding agent headlessly, with shared state maintained on the filesystem between iterations:

```bash
while :; do
  cat PROMPT.md | claude-code
done
```

Each iteration:
1. Read current instructions from `PROMPT.md`
2. Run the agent with those instructions
3. Agent reads/writes shared filesystem state
4. Loop back

### Files That Carry State Across Iterations

| File | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `@PROMPT.md` | Current instructions for this iteration |
| `@fix_plan.md` | Prioritized TODO list — the institutional memory |
| `@AGENT.md` | Learned operational knowledge (agent self-updates this) |
| `@specs/*` | Technical specifications |

The key insight: **state lives in files, not context**. Each iteration starts with a fresh context window. The agent reads its prior work from the filesystem and picks up where it left off — no context window accumulation, no degradation.

### Huntley's Core Philosophy

> "There seems to be an obsession in the programming community with the perfect prompt. There is no such thing as a perfect prompt."

Source: https://ghuntley.com/ralph/

The obsession with prompt engineering is misplaced. The loop is what matters. An imperfect prompt that runs 50 times with feedback will outperform a perfect prompt that runs once.

Cardinal rule: **"Only one thing [per loop iteration]."** Each loop iteration has a single, atomic task. Compound tasks in one iteration lead to partial failures that are hard to recover from.

### Stop Conditions

The loop terminates when:
- The TODO list in `@fix_plan.md` empties
- The codebase becomes broken (operator resets with `git reset --hard`)
- Goals are achieved
- Operator manually intervenes

No automatic success detection beyond empty-TODO — the operator defines done.

### "Everything Is a Ralph Loop" (ghuntley.com/loop/)

Source: https://ghuntley.com/loop/

Development as pottery: "if something isn't right then i just throw it back on the wheel"

Four components Huntley identifies:
1. **Context Engineering** — what flows into each context window
2. **Monolithic Architecture** — shared filesystem = shared state
3. **Continuous Verification** — compiler/test feedback at each iteration
4. **Evolutionary Development** — the codebase self-improves across iterations

### Ralph Codebase Porting: Three Phases

Source: https://agent-wars.com/news/2026-03-15-ralph-autonomous-subagent-codebase-porting

For porting a codebase from one language/framework to another, the Ralph loop executes in three phases:

1. **Compression**: Subagents study the source codebase, producing Markdown specs
2. **Citation**: A PRD with inline citations — citations act as lazy-load context triggers
3. **Execution**: Agent executes the port one task at a time, guided by the specs

Citations as lazy-loading: the agent only fetches source context when it hits a relevant citation, rather than loading everything upfront. This dramatically reduces context overhead.

---

## The Verification Gate: "Something That Can Say No"

### @mosyaseen's Point (from the June 7 thread)

> "The other half is putting something in the loop that can say no: a test, a type check, a real error."

This is the critical structural insight. The loop has two halves:
- The forward pass: agent generates code
- The verification gate: automated check that either passes or emits a "no"

Without the verification gate, the loop either runs forever or requires human evaluation. With it, the loop is **autonomous and deterministic**: it terminates when the gate passes.

### Boris Cherny's Stop Hooks

Boris's mechanism for this in Claude Code: **stop hooks**. A hook that runs when a turn completes, checks test results, and if they fail, inserts an instruction for Claude to continue. The model never stops until the gate passes.

From Every.to transcript:
> "You can just make the model keep going until the thing is done."

This is not "tell Claude to keep going" — it's a **hook that automatically tells Claude to keep going** based on objective verification.

### Simon Willison on Agentic Loop Design

Source: https://simonwillison.net/2025/Sep/30/designing-agentic-loops/

> "The art of using them well is to carefully design the tools and loop for them to use."

Willison's checklist for agentic loops:
- AGENTS.md for tool documentation
- Tightly scoped credentials (test environment, budget limits)
- Run in sandboxed environments (GitHub Codespaces, Docker)
- Ideal problems: clear success criteria + trial-and-error friendly

The "trial-and-error friendly" criterion is exactly the verification gate requirement: if a problem can't be automatically evaluated, it can't close the loop.

---

## General Anatomy of an Agent-Prompting Loop

Synthesizing across all sources:

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                  SPEC FILES                      │
│  VISION.md / CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md / PROMPT.md  │
│  (persisted goals + learned constraints)         │
└──────────────────────┬──────────────────────────┘
                       │ read on each iteration
                       ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              SUPERVISOR / ORCHESTRATOR           │
│  (Boris: stop-hook layer / steipete: claw /      │
│   Huntley: the while loop itself)                │
│  - decomposes task                               │
│  - dispatches to worker agents                   │
│  - receives outputs                              │
└──────────────────────┬──────────────────────────┘
                       │ task + context
                       ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              CODING AGENT(S)                     │
│  (claude-code / codex / parallel fleet)          │
│  - executes task                                 │
│  - writes to filesystem                          │
│  - fresh context window per iteration            │
└──────────────────────┬──────────────────────────┘
                       │ output / changed files
```

### Core Pattern

Source: https://ghuntley.com/ralph/

The Ralph loop is the simplest possible agentic loop — a bash while loop calling a coding agent headlessly, with shared state maintained on the filesystem between iterations:

```bash
while :; do
  cat PROMPT.md | claude-code
done
```

Each iteration:
1. Read current instructions from `PROMPT.md`
2. Run the agent with those instructions
3. Agent reads/writes shared filesystem state
4. Loop back

### Files That Carry State Across Iterations

| File | Purpose |
|---|---|

| `@fix_plan.md` | Prioritized TODO list — the institutional memory |
| `@AGENT.md` | Learned operational knowledge (agent self-updates this) |
| `@specs/*` | Technical specifications |

The key insight: **state lives in files, not context**. Each iteration starts with a fresh context window. The agent reads its prior work from the filesystem and picks up where it left off — no context window accumulation, no degradation.

> "There seems to be an obsession in the programming community with the perfect prompt. There is no such thing as a perfect prompt."

The loop terminates when:
- The TODO list in `@fix_plan.md` empties
- The codebase becomes broken (operator resets with `git reset --hard`)
- Goals are achieved
- Operator manually intervenes

No automatic success detection beyond empty-TODO — the operator defines done.

1. **Compression**: Subagents study the source codebase, producing Markdown specs

content.text:
Verified against your links. WorkOS/Acquired confirms the core: *"Now he doesn't even prompt Claude directly. He writes loops — automated workflows that prompt Claude and figure out what to build next"* and *"hundreds of Claude instances monitoring Twitter feedback, GitHub issues, and Slack."* Here's the whole picture.

---

## What Boris actually means

The quote isn't motivational fluff — it's a literal description of his workflow. The progression he describes:

**write code → write prompts → write loops.**

He no longer sits in a chat typing prompts to one Claude. He writes a *harness* — a script or hook config — that repeatedly invokes Claude, feeds it state, checks the result, and re-invokes it until a goal is met. The loop is the artifact you author now. The agent is just the thing the loop calls.

This is the same shift Geoffrey Huntley (who 🫡'd the thread) calls the **Ralph loop**, and that Simon Willison calls **"designing agentic loops."**

## The anatomy (every version of this has the same 4 parts)

```
SPEC ───► AGENT ───► VERIFICATION GATE ───► (pass? stop : feed error back)
 ▲                                                        │
 └────────────── state on filesystem ◄───────────────────┘
```

1. **A spec file** — Steinberger's `VISION.md`, Boris's `CLAUDE.md`, Huntley's `PROMPT.md`/`fix_plan.md`. Persistent goal + accumulated rules. Survives context resets; the agent re-reads it every iteration. Boris updates his CLAUDE.md *multiple times a week* — every time the agent screws up, he adds a rule.
2. **The agent** — claude/codex run headlessly, often a *fresh context each iteration* (state lives in files, not the context window — that's the key trick that stops degradation).
3. **The verification gate** — this is the half everyone forgets. @mosyaseen nailed it in your thread: *"put something in the loop that can say no: a test, a type check, a real error. A loop with nothing to push back is the agent agreeing with itself on repeat."* Tests, `tsc --noEmit`, compiler, linter, CI. The gate's "no" *becomes the next prompt.*
4. **The stop condition** — gate passes, or TODO list empties. Without it the loop runs forever or needs you babysitting.

Steinberger's *"claw supervising my codexes"* is the supervisor variant: one orchestrator agent (his OpenClaw "claw") dispatches work to N worker agents (codex), collects outputs, judges them. His own caveat matches mosyaseen's: *"it won't fix system architecture for ya, so you still need BRAIN as master model"* — the loop handles iteration, a strong model still owns judgment.

## How you actually do it

**Tier 0 — the Ralph one-liner** (dumbest thing that works):
```bash
while :; do cat PROMPT.md | claude -p; done
```
`PROMPT.md` says "read fix_plan.md, do the next ONE task, run the tests, update fix_plan.md." Cardinal rule: **one thing per iteration.** State accumulates in files.

**Tier 1 — loop with a real gate** (the version worth running):
```bash
while ! npm test --silent; do
  claude -p "Tests are failing. Read VISION.md for intent. \
  Fix the next failure. Run no other changes." \
  --allowedTools "Edit,Bash(npm test)"
done
```
The gate (`npm test`) *is* the loop condition. It literally cannot exit on broken code.

**Tier 2 — Boris's stop-hook version (in Claude Code, no bash):** configure a **Stop hook** that runs your tests when a turn ends; if they fail, it blocks the stop and tells Claude to keep going. The model self-iterates to green without you in the seat. This is exactly the `/loop` + goal-hook machinery — *which you already have in this repo.*

**Tier 3 — supervisor/fleet:** one orchestrator decomposes into a TODO, fans work out to parallel agents (worktrees so they don't collide), each with its own gate, synthesizes. That's Boris's "hundreds of quads" and Steinberger's claw→codex.

## You're already holding most of the tooling

Worth saying plainly — your `my-pi` setup is built for this:
- **`/loop`** skill — runs a prompt/command on an interval or self-paced. That's Tier 0/1.
- **`harness-loop`** skill — explicitly "goal runs, eval-gate, PROGRESS.md/PLAN.md orchestration, quality gates." That's the gated loop, packaged.
- **The `/goal` you just set** — a Stop hook blocking exit until a condition holds. That *is* Boris's stop-hook pattern; you're inside one right now.
- **`project-sdlc`** owns `VISION.md` — Steinberger's exact spec-file move.

So the answer to "how do I loop-prompt my agents": write a `VISION.md`, pick a gate you trust (`test:extension-gate` here), and drive it with `harness-loop`/`/loop` + a Stop-hook goal. Don't chase the perfect prompt — Huntley: *"there is no such thing as a perfect prompt."* Chase the gate.

## Sources

**Solid (verified):**
- WorkOS / Acquired Unplugged — Boris interview takeaways: https://workos.com/blog/boris-cherny-claude-code-acquired-interview-takeaways
- Acquired Unplugged full video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RkQQ7WEor7w
- Geoffrey Huntley — Ralph loop: https://ghuntley.com/ralph/ · https://ghuntley.com/loop/
- Simon Willison — Designing agentic loops: https://simonwillison.net/2025/Sep/30/designing-agentic-loops/
- Steinberger — Commanding Your Claude Code Army: https://steipete.me/posts/2025/commanding-your-claude-code-army
- Your thread: the mosyaseen "something that can say no" reply is the most important comment in it.

**Secondary (treat as paraphrase, not gospel — couldn't fully verify):** every.to AI&I transcript, officechai, howborisusesclaudecode.com, karozieminski substack. They agree with the verified sources but I didn't confirm the exact quotes.
